facts: Rueda is a Spanish DOP in Castile and León, known mainly for white wines based on the Verdejo grape.
The vineyards sit on a flat high plain at 2,000 to 2,560 feet above sea level, with the Duero River flowing through.
The climate is continental with some Atlantic influence, with long hot summers, cold winters, and frost and hail risks in winter and spring.
Irrigation is only allowed under special circumstances, and vines are often trained close to the ground to resist strong winds.
Gran Vino de Rueda comes from vineyards over 30 years old, with yields under 6,500 kg/ha and a transformation ratio of 65%.
American Viticultural Areas (AVAs) are based on distinct local geography, climate and soil, and have been set up by federal regulators since 1978.
For an AVA to appear on a label, at least 85% of the grapes must come from within it.
A wine labelled with a varietal must be at least 75% of that grape, and Oregon requires 90% for certain varietals such as Pinot Noir.
Columbia Valley is a large AVA covering much of central and southern Washington and reaching into northern Oregon, established in 1984.
It holds about 99% of Washington's vineyard acreage and contains eighteen appellations, including Walla Walla Valley, Yakima Valley, Red Mountain and Horse Heaven Hills.
The Cascade Range casts a rain shadow, so some areas get less than 6 inches of rain a year and vineyards depend on irrigation.
Growers use water from the Columbia, Snake, Yakima and Walla Walla Rivers to control the timing and amount of water the vines receive.
Deep winter freezes are the main climate threat, with temperatures able to fall from 40°F to below 0°F in hours.
Finger Lakes is an AVA in upstate New York, set up in 1982, and about 80 percent of the state's wine comes from it.
Deep lakes hold their warmth and moderate temperatures, keeping some vineyards 10 to 15°F warmer than sites half a mile away.
Lake effect snow cover protects vines from winter freeze, and cool spring breezes delay bud-break until the danger of frost has passed.
Riesling is one of the most successful varieties, and the region is often compared to the German regions along the Rhine.
Growers plant European Vitis vinifera, native American Vitis labrusca and French-American hybrid grapes.
Cayuga Lake and Seneca Lake were set up as sub-appellations, in 1988 and 2003 respectively.
Napa Valley was established as the nation's second AVA in 1981 and covers all of Napa County except the portion northeast of Putah Creek and Lake Berryessa.
Grape varieties grown include Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Merlot and Zinfandel.
As of 2024, there are seventeen sub-AVAs within Napa Valley, and the Oakville and Rutherford AVAs lie on the Rutherford Bench.
The open southern end of the valley floor is cooler because of San Pablo Bay, while the sheltered northern end is often much warmer.
Soils in the south are mainly sediments from San Pablo Bay, while the north has a large volume of volcanic lava and ash.
The climate is Mediterranean, with hot dry summers and cool wet winters, and daily summer fog that usually lingers until mid-morning.
County names qualify automatically as legal appellations of origin, so Sonoma County wines need no TTB registration to use the name.
Sonoma County has 19 AVAs, reflecting its wide variety of climate and soil conditions.
The most common varieties planted are Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon and Pinot Noir, and the area is also known for Merlot and Zinfandel.
Russian River Valley is marked by cooling coastal fog that arrives in the evening or early morning and retreats before noon.
Russian River Valley is known for cool climate varieties, notably Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
The Petaluma Gap lets cool ocean air flow inland, and with San Pablo Bay it makes the region suited to Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Syrah.
Willamette Valley is Oregon's largest AVA, established in 1983, and has a cool, moist climate recognized worldwide for Pinot Noir.
Most producers do not irrigate, which supports deep-rooted vines and rapid ripening from some water stress.
Most vineyards sit on southeast-facing slopes, and soils are generally marine sedimentary, volcanic and loess.
Winters are cool and wet and summers dry and warm, with heat above 90°F on only 5 to 15 days per year.
Yamhill-Carlton District and McMinnville only allow vineyards between 200 and 1,000 feet in elevation to use the appellation name.
